title: How to Reduce LLM Costs in 2026 (A Practical Guide)
summary: Reduce LLM API costs in 2026 with prompt caching, model routing, batch APIs, and output caps, plus a cost calculator, cache discounts, and the cheapest APIs.
body_markdown:
Large language models get cheaper per token every quarter, yet many teams watch their monthly API bill climb anyway. The reason is arithmetic: prices fall, but the number of model calls and tokens per task rises faster. The good news: ten well-understood LLM cost optimization techniques can reduce LLM API costs on a typical bill by 80 percent or more without lower output quality.


This guide ranks each technique by typical saving and shows the provider rates behind it (checked on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20 against the OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek docs). It gives you an LLM API cost calculator you can run by hand, compares prompt caching discounts by provider, names the cheapest LLM APIs this month, and ends with a worked example that takes a $1,800 monthly bill down to about $231.


> **TL;DR:** To reduce LLM API costs, cache the repeated prompt prefix (cache reads cost 0.1x input on Anthropic, up to 95 percent off on OpenAI), route easy tasks to cheaper models, cap output, trim context, and batch non-urgent work at 50 percent off. Our worked example cuts a bill by 87 percent. Start with[prompt caching](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/prompt-caching) .


---


## How Do You Reduce LLM API Costs?


**To reduce LLM API costs, cache the repeated part of every prompt, send easy tasks to a cheaper model, cap the length of each answer, trim the context, and move work that can wait to a batch API at 50 percent off.** Measure cost per completed task before and after each change. Together, these levers often cut a typical bill by 80 percent or more.


The table ranks the ten techniques by how much they usually save and how much work they take. "Typical saving" means the saving on the part of the bill that the technique touches, not on the whole bill. The sources are the provider docs and research papers linked in each section below.


Rank Technique Typical saving Effort Source

2 **Model routing** More than 2x lower cost in RouteLLM, up to 98 percent in FrugalGPT Medium[RouteLLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665) ,[FrugalGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176) papers

Two rules hold across the whole table. First, the techniques stack, because each one attacks a different term in the cost equation. Second, the order matters: caching and batching are nearly free to add, while routing and fine-tuning need an evaluation set before you can trust them. The rest of this guide explains each row, then combines them on one bill.


---


## Why LLM Bills Grow Even as Token Prices Fall


**An LLM bill is the product of three numbers: tokens per call, price per token, and calls per task.** Providers keep pushing the price per token down, but modern AI applications keep pushing calls per task up. One user request now fans out into planning, retrieval, generation, tool use, and verification steps, so a single task can use many times the tokens of one chat reply.


Anthropic measured this effect on its own systems. In its write-up of a[multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) , the company reported that agents use about 4 times the tokens of a chat interaction, and multi-agent systems use about 15 times. The unit price drops while the total climbs.


This is why the right unit of measurement is **cost per completed task** , not cost per token. A per-token dashboard can look flat while spend rises, because it misses the growing call count. Long[context windows](https://www.taskade.com/blog/context-window-history) made the problem worse: when a model accepts a million tokens, teams start to send far more than the task needs. And because a[token](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/token) is the unit you pay for, every technique below works by sending fewer tokens, paying less for each one, or making fewer calls.


The cost equation, written out:


```text
cost per task  =  calls per task
× ( uncached input tokens × input rate
+ cached input tokens   × cache read rate
+ cache write tokens    × cache write rate
+ output tokens         × output rate )
× ( 1 + retry rate )


```


Every technique in this guide moves one term. Caching moves cached tokens to a cheaper rate. Routing lowers every rate. Output caps shrink output tokens. Context trimming shrinks input tokens. Batching and off-peak pricing halve the rates for work that can wait. Structured outputs and loop caps shrink the retry rate and the call count.

## Why Prefill, Decode, and Caching Set the Price You Pay


**Providers price input, output, and cached tokens differently because each one uses the GPU differently.** During prefill, the model reads all input tokens in parallel, which is fast and cheap per token. During decode, the model writes output one token at a time, which keeps the GPU busy longer per token. A cached prefix skips most of the prefill work, so it costs the least.


That is why output tokens cost several times more than input tokens in almost every price list, and why cache reads cost a small fraction of fresh input. On the DeepSeek API, output costs 3 times the cache-miss input rate. Many frontier models charge 4 to 5 times. For example, Anthropic lists one of its mid-tier models at $3 input and $15 output per million tokens.


This supply-side view explains why the techniques in this guide work, and it is worth one deeper read.[Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS)](https://www.taskade.com/blog/inference-as-a-service) is our pillar on the serving stack: who sells tokens, how prefill and decode set the price of each line on your bill, and why cache-hit rates matter more than headline prices. For a plain-English version with a glossary for buyers, read[AI inference explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-inference-explained) . And to follow one request from the power grid to the bill, see[how AI data centers work](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-data-centers-explained) .

## How to Measure LLM Cost Per Task Before You Optimize


**Measure cost per completed task by logging the token counts that each API response returns, grouping them by task type, and dividing total spend by the number of tasks that succeeded.** Without this baseline, you cannot tell which technique helped, and a cheaper call that fails and repeats can raise your bill while each call looks cheaper.


Every major provider returns the numbers you need in the response body. Log them on every call, together with the model name, the task type, and whether the task succeeded.


Provider Cached input field Cache write field Other fields to log


Anthropic` cache_read_input_tokens`` cache_creation_input_tokens`` input_tokens` ,` output_tokens`


OpenAI` cached_tokens` in the input token details` cache_write_tokens` Input, output, and reasoning tokens


Google Gemini Cached content token count in usage metadata Not billed as a write on implicit caching Prompt and candidate token counts


DeepSeek Cache-hit tokens in usage No write charge Cache-miss and output tokens


Three measurement habits make the numbers useful:


1. **Divide by successful tasks, not calls.** A task that needs three retries costs three calls, and the per-call view hides that.
2. **Change one lever at a time.** Compare one week before and one week after each change, on the same task types.
3. **Measure quality next to cost.** Keep a small evaluation set and score it after each change.[Agent evals explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/agent-evals-explained) covers how to build one.


The full 20-task protocol, with the cost-per-accepted-result formula, is in[what one AI task really costs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-cost-per-task) . The main lesson: the spread between the cheapest and the most expensive way to finish the same task can be far wider than the spread between list prices, because calls per task and retries vary more than rates do.

## LLM API Cost Calculator: Price One Request by Hand


**To calculate the cost of one LLM API request, multiply each token type by its own rate and add the results: uncached input, cached input, cache writes, and output, each divided by one million.** Multiply by requests per month to get the bill. The math takes one minute, and it shows which lever matters before you change any code.


Most online calculators ask for one input number and one output number. That hides the line that moves the most: cached input. A provider can bill the same 5,000-token preamble at the full input rate or at 5 percent of it, and the only difference is whether the prefix matched an earlier call.


Here is one request priced by hand on a frontier model, using the OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol rates from the[OpenAI pricing page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing) on 2026-10-20.


```text
ONE REQUEST, PRICED BY HAND                  (rates per 1M tokens)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Prompt   6,000 tokens  =  5,000 stable prefix + 1,000 new tokens
Answer     400 tokens
Rates    input $2.00 · cache write $2.50 · cached $0.10 · output $10.00  NO CACHING AT ALL  input      6,000 × $2.00  ÷ 1M   =  $0.01200  output       400 × $10.00 ÷ 1M   =  $0.00400  total                            =  $0.01600   (1.60 cents)
FIRST CALL (writes the prefix to the cache)  write      5,000 × $2.50  ÷ 1M   =  $0.01250  input      1,000 × $2.00  ÷ 1M   =  $0.00200  output       400 × $10.00 ÷ 1M   =  $0.00400  total                            =  $0.01850   (1.85 cents)
EVERY LATER CALL (cache hit on the prefix)  cached     5,000 × $0.10  ÷ 1M   =  $0.00050  input      1,000 × $2.00  ÷ 1M   =  $0.00200  output       400 × $10.00 ÷ 1M   =  $0.00400  total                            =  $0.00650   (0.65 cents)
Saving per cache-hit call vs no caching          =  59 percent  Output share of the bill after the cache hit     =  62 percent  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```


Two numbers in that block drive the rest of this guide. The cache hit cuts the request by 59 percent, so caching comes first. After the hit, output is 62 percent of what is left, so output control comes next. The one-time write premium is paid back by the first cache hit.


The same request costs very different amounts on different price lists. The table prices 1,000 calls of that request on five models, from each provider's official pricing page on 2026-10-20. DeepSeek and Gemini implicit caching charge no cache write, so their first call costs the plain input rate.

To run the same math in code, log the usage fields that each response returns and price them with one function:


Python


```text
def request_cost(uncached_in, cached_in, cache_write, output, rates):
"""Rates are dollars per 1M tokens for each token type."""
return (
uncached_in * rates["input"]
+ cached_in * rates["cached"]
+ cache_write * rates["write"]
+ output * rates["output"]
) / 1_000_000  sol = {"input": 2.00, "cached": 0.10, "write": 2.50, "output": 10.00}  print(request_cost(1_000, 5_000, 0, 400, sol))  # 0.0065 dollars per call
```


Multiply the result by your monthly requests and by one plus your retry rate, and you have an LLM API cost calculator that matches your real traffic instead of a guess. For the theory behind each rate, the[inference cost](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/inference-cost) wiki entry explains where the money goes on the server side.

**A per-token calculator misses six price rules that the official pricing pages state in their footnotes.** Each one can move a real bill by 10 percent or more, and none shows up when you multiply one input rate by one output rate.

The[tokenizer](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/tokenizer) entry explains why two models count the same sentence differently, and the[token](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/token) entry covers the unit itself.

## Technique 1: Prompt Caching (Cut Repeated-Prefix Input Cost)


**Prompt caching bills a repeated prompt prefix at a fraction of the base input price, and it is the highest-leverage change for any app with a stable preamble.** Most requests share the same opening: a system prompt, tool definitions, a style guide, or retrieved documents. The provider keeps that prefix after the first call and serves it cheaply on every call that follows.


The rates below come from each provider's documentation, checked on 2026-10-19. A multiplier is relative to the model's base input price.

OpenAI, GPT-5.6 and later 0.1x on most models (0.05x on one) 1.25x 1,024 tokens On by default, 30-minute lifetime


OpenAI, earlier models Model-specific discount No write charge Varies with tools and schemas On by default, in-memory or 24-hour retention


Google Gemini Discount passed through automatically No write charge on implicit caching 2,048 to 4,096 tokens, by model Implicit caching on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer


DeepSeek Cache-hit rate (about 3 percent of the cache-miss rate on deepseek-v4-pro) No write charge Automatic On by default


OpenAI summarizes the effect as cached input "discounted up to 95%." Anthropic notes that the cache lifetime refreshes for free each time a request reads the cached content, so steady traffic keeps a prefix warm. Anthropic also notes that the lifetime counts from the start of the request, so a long streamed answer uses part of the 5-minute window.

The read discount is only half of the picture. OpenAI (GPT-5.6 and later) and Anthropic charge 1.25x the input rate to write a 5-minute cache entry, and Anthropic charges 2x for a 1-hour entry. DeepSeek and Gemini implicit caching charge no write. Gemini explicit caching adds an hourly storage fee instead. So a prefix that is reused once is a small win everywhere, and a prefix that is reused hundreds of times per hour is a large win everywhere. The[prompt caching](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/prompt-caching) wiki entry and the[KV cache](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/kv-cache) entry explain the mechanism that makes the discount possible.


### When does the cache write premium pay off?


**On Anthropic, a 5-minute cache write pays for itself after one reuse, and a 1-hour write pays for itself after two reuses.** The arithmetic: without caching, two calls with the same prefix cost 2.0x. With a 5-minute cache, they cost 1.25x for the write plus 0.1x for the read, which is 1.35x. With a 1-hour cache, three calls cost 2.0x plus 0.1x plus 0.1x, which is 2.2x, against 3.0x uncached. Use the 1-hour cache when calls with the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart.


### Put stable content first


**Caching is a prefix match, so any byte change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it.** Put stable content first and volatile content last: system prompt, then tool definitions, then reference documents, then the conversation, then the user's question.


A silent cache miss is the most common failure. If you insert the current date into the system prompt, shuffle the order of tool definitions, or serialize a dictionary without sorted keys, the prefix bytes differ on every request and nothing caches. Check the cached-token field in each response: if it stays at zero across calls with the same prefix, a non-deterministic prompt builder is breaking your prefix. Designing prompts so that the stable part stays frozen is the core discipline of[context engineering](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/context-engineering) .


### How a cache entry lives and expires


**A prompt cache entry is created by the first call, kept warm by every read inside its lifetime, and lost when the lifetime passes with no read or when an early byte of the prompt changes.** That lifecycle explains most real cache-hit rates. Steady traffic keeps an entry warm for hours at the read price. Bursty traffic pays the write premium again after every quiet gap.


Three habits raise the hit rate on real traffic:


- **Match the lifetime to the traffic.** If calls with the same prefix arrive minutes apart, the default lifetime is enough. If they arrive an hour apart, pay for the longer lifetime, or send a cheap keep-warm call only when the math says it pays.
- **Share one prefix across features.** Two features with slightly different system prompts build two cache entries. One shared preamble followed by a short feature-specific block builds one.
- **Route the same prefix to the same place.** OpenAI documents a` prompt_cache_key` parameter that influences routing, and says it matters most on models before GPT-5.6. A key does not guarantee a hit. Read your provider's docs for its version of this control.


### Caching on hybrid models (Kimi K3) is coarser


**On a hybrid model such as Kimi K3, a cached prefix is reused only from the nearest saved checkpoint, not to the exact token.** Kimi K3 mixes 69 linear-attention (KDA) layers with 24 Gated MLA layers. The MLA layers keep a per-token cache that can be reused to the exact token, but the KDA layers keep one fixed-size state per sequence, so the server resumes from the nearest saved copy of that state and prefills the rest again. The rule stays the same and matters more: keep the shared prefix long and identical.[Inference-as-a-Service explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/inference-as-a-service) covers the serving side in depth.


Hybrid designs exist because they lower serving cost elsewhere. The linear-attention layers keep a fixed-size state instead of a cache that grows with every token, so long contexts need far less GPU memory. The trade for a buyer is a coarser cache. Baseten's talk on serving trillion-parameter models walks through how a host splits these layers across GPUs and why the two caches need two memory allocators.

## Technique 2: Model Routing (Send Easy Tasks to Cheap Models)


**Model routing sends each task to the cheapest model that can meet the quality bar, and it works because most production traffic is simple.** A small model can cost a fraction of a frontier model per token. When most requests are short classifications, extractions, summaries, and FAQ answers, a frontier model on every call means premium rates for work a small model handles well.


Two research results set the expectation. The[RouteLLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665) paper trained routers on human preference data and reported cost cuts of more than 2 times in some cases without lower response quality. The earlier[FrugalGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176) paper used a cascade, trying cheap models first and escalating only when a scorer rejected the answer, and reported that it matched the best single model with up to 98 percent lower cost on its benchmarks.


The price gap between tiers is real. In[what GPT is and where GPT-6 fits](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-is-gpt) , the larger model lists at $2/$10 and the smaller one at $0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens, a 20x gap. But the assumption that the cheap tier is always worse is worth testing: when we gave nine models the same app request, the cheapest model in the field built the best-looking app twice. See[best AI model for building apps](https://www.taskade.com/blog/best-model-for-apps) .


```text
┌─────────────────────┐
incoming task ──▶│  complexity check   │
└──────────┬──────────┘
│
simple ◀─────────┴─────────▶ complex
│                           │
▼                           ▼
┌──────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
│  small model     │       │  frontier model  │
│  low rate        │       │  premium rate    │
│  summaries, FAQs │       │  hard reasoning  │
└──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘


```


There are three common router designs:


- **Rules.** Route by task type, input length, or the feature that made the call. Simple, fast, and easy to debug.
- **Classifier.** A small model or a trained classifier scores each request and picks a tier. This is the RouteLLM approach.
- **Cascade.** Try the cheap model first, score the answer with a check (a schema, a test, or a judge model), and escalate only when the check fails. This is the FrugalGPT approach.


The trade-off to watch is quality. Route too aggressively and you push tasks to a model that cannot handle them, which triggers retries and erases the gain. A cascade also pays twice for every escalated task, so it saves money only when most tasks pass on the first try. Start conservative, measure per-task quality, and widen the cheap lane only where accuracy holds. Choosing the right[reasoning effort](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/reasoning-effort) per tier is part of the same decision, since a lower effort setting on a capable model is itself a cost lever. For agent-specific routing, see our companion guide on[AI agent cost optimization](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization) .


### Router or cascade: which one saves more?


**A router decides before the call, and a cascade decides after it, so a router saves more when you can predict difficulty and a cascade saves more when you can cheaply check the answer.** Most production systems end up with both: rules for the obvious task types, and a cascade for the mixed middle.


Design Extra cost per task Extra latency Best when

Trained classifier One small classification call Small Traffic is mixed and you have labeled or preference data


Cascade with a check A cheap call on every task, plus the check High on escalated tasks only Most tasks pass the cheap model, and a schema or test can grade the answer

A cascade has a simple break-even point. If the cheap model costs 5 percent of the frontier model per task, the cascade saves money until almost every task escalates. The real limit is quality and latency, not the math:

```text
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Frontier model on every task            =  $10.00
Cheap model on every task               =   $0.50
Cascade cost = $0.50 + (escalation rate × $10.00)     escalation  10 percent   →   $1.50     85 percent saved  escalation  30 percent   →   $3.50     65 percent saved  escalation  60 percent   →   $6.50     35 percent saved  escalation  95 percent   →  $10.00     break-even  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  A judge-model check adds its own cost. A schema or unit test adds ~0.
```


Cheap does not always mean worse. On the TSK-Bench scoreboard, where each model built the same real app and was then used like a customer would use it, several model families from different price tiers tied on task completion. That is the evidence a router needs: a measured quality score on your own task, next to the price.


The full method and per-family results live on the[TSK benchmark page](https://www.taskade.com/tsk) , with family pages such as[GPT on TSK](https://www.taskade.com/tsk/gpt) ,[DeepSeek on TSK](https://www.taskade.com/tsk/deepseek) , and[Kimi on TSK](https://www.taskade.com/tsk/kimi) . The RouteLLM talk below explains how a router learns which queries a cheaper model can handle.


If you build agents in Taskade, you can pin the model for each agent by hand, which is rules-based routing with no code: a tagging agent on a low-cost model, a planning agent on a frontier model.

## Technique 3: Control Output Length (Output Tokens Cost the Most)


**Output tokens cost 3 to 5 times more than input tokens on most price lists, so every unneeded word in an answer is the most expensive token on your bill.** Cutting average output from 300 to 200 tokens removes a third of the output cost. That one change can save more than a large cut to the prompt.


Output grows quietly. Models add preambles ("Great question!"), restate the question, add caveats, and close with offers to help further. Reasoning models add a second source: thinking tokens, which most providers bill at the output rate even when you never see them.[Reasoning models](https://www.taskade.com/blog/reasoning-models) explains how that hidden output grows with task difficulty.


Lever What it does Where to set it


` max_tokens` or the output token limit Hard cap on the answer length API request parameter


Length instructions "Answer in 2 sentences" or "Return only the label" System prompt


Reasoning effort Lower thinking budget on easy tasks API request parameter, per task type


Stop sequences End the answer at a known marker API request parameter


Structured output schema Return fields, not prose Response format parameter


Treat` max_tokens` as a safety net, not the main control. A hard cap cuts an answer mid-sentence, and a cut-off answer often forces a retry, which costs more than the tokens you saved. Clear length instructions and a schema shape the answer, and the cap catches the rare runaway. For classification and extraction tasks, ask for the label or the fields only. That can turn a 300-token answer into a 10-token answer.

## Technique 4: Trim the Context (Shorter Prompts, Fewer Tokens)


**Trimming context cuts input tokens directly, and input is where most apps overspend by volume.** A bigger context window does not raise the price per token, but filling it does. Passing a full document set or a full conversation history on every call multiplies input cost and can degrade the answer, an effect called[context rot](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/context-rot) , where relevant details get lost in noise.


Four habits keep context lean:


- **Retrieve, do not dump.** Pull only the passages relevant to the current question instead of the whole knowledge base. This is the core idea behind[retrieval-augmented generation](https://www.taskade.com/blog/rag-retrieval-history) , and it cuts input tokens sharply. Tune the number of retrieved chunks: going from 20 chunks to 5 cuts that part of the prompt by three quarters.
- **Compact old turns.** In long conversations, summarize earlier exchanges rather than resend them word for word.[Context compaction](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai-agents/context-compaction) replaces a long history with a short summary the model can still act on.
- **Drop stale tool results.** Once an agent has used a tool's output, the raw result rarely needs to stay in context for the rest of the run.
- **Audit tool definitions.** Every tool schema you attach is sent on every call. Attach only the tools the current step can use.


Prompt compression goes one step further. Microsoft Research's[LLMLingua](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05736) removes low-information tokens from a prompt with a small model and reported up to 20x compression with little performance loss on its benchmarks. Compression and caching pull in different directions, though: a compressed prompt that changes on every call does not cache. Compress the variable part and cache the stable part.


Shorter context is a double win: you pay for fewer tokens, and you often get a more accurate answer because the model is not distracted. If your app keeps state across sessions, pair retrieval with a durable memory layer so that the live prompt stays small. ## Technique 7: Structured Outputs (Stop Paying for Retries)


**Structured outputs make the model return JSON that matches a schema you define, which nearly eliminates the malformed answers that force a retry.** Every retry is a second full-price call for the same task, so a lower failure rate cuts spend directly. This is the quietest lever, because the waste is invisible on a per-call dashboard, yet it compounds fast at scale.


OpenAI describes[Structured Outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) as a feature that makes the model always follow your supplied JSON Schema. One 2026 analysis found that loose JSON mode fails schema validation[5 to 10 percent of the time](https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/ai/20260506-llm-structured-output/) , while strictly enforced structured outputs fail less than 0.1 percent of the time. Fewer retries also mean less defensive parsing code, so the saving shows up in both your token bill and your engineering time.


A schema also controls output length. A response with three typed fields cannot ramble, so structured outputs double as an output cap. If your application feeds model output into a database, an API call, or another model, make structured outputs the default.

## Technique 8: Semantic Caching (Skip the Model Call Entirely)


**Semantic caching stores past answers in your own application and returns a stored answer when a new question means the same thing, so no model call happens at all.** Prompt caching makes a call cheaper. Semantic caching removes the call. It fits workloads where many users ask the same questions in different words, such as support assistants, internal help desks, and product FAQ bots.


The mechanism: embed each incoming question, search a vector store for a past question above a similarity threshold, and return the stored answer on a hit. On a miss, call the model, then store the new question, its embedding, and the answer.


Semantic caching has real risks, so add it with care:


- **False hits.** Two questions can look similar and need different answers ("cancel my order" versus "cancel my subscription"). Start with a strict similarity threshold and loosen it only after you review false hits by hand.
- **Stale answers.** Give each stored answer an expiry, and clear the cache when the underlying facts change, such as prices or policies.
- **Private data.** Never return a stored answer that contains one user's data to another user. Scope the cache by account, or cache only answers that contain no personal data.
- **Embedding cost.** Each lookup costs an embedding call and a vector search. That is cheap next to a frontier model call, but measure it.


Your saving equals your hit rate times the cost of the calls you skip, minus the lookup cost. Measure the hit rate for two weeks before you count on it.

## Technique 9: Cap Agent Loops and Retries


**Agent loops are where LLM spend runs away, because an agent decides for itself how many calls a task needs.** A stuck agent can call the same tool again and again, re-read the same file, or retry a failed step with the full context each time. Each loop iteration resends the growing history, so the cost of the tenth step can be many times the cost of the first.


Four caps keep agent spend bounded:


1. **A step limit.** Stop the run after a fixed number of tool calls and return what the agent has so far.
2. **A token budget per run.** Stop or escalate to a human when a run passes a set token count.
3. **A retry limit with backoff.** Retry a failed call at most two or three times. Escalate to a larger model only through your router, not as a blind retry.
4. **Deterministic code for deterministic work.** Validation, formatting, date math, and lookups belong in code, not in a model call.


The stateless nature of most LLM APIs means every token you resend is a token you pay for again. That is why context compaction (Technique 4) and loop caps work together: compaction keeps each step small, and caps keep the number of steps small. For a deeper look at agent spend, see[AI agent cost optimization](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization) .

## How to Reduce LLM API Costs for AI Agents


**To reduce LLM API costs for AI agents, shrink what each step resends and cap how many steps run.** An agent is a loop. Every step sends the system prompt, the tool definitions, and the whole history so far, then appends the new result. Without compaction, the input of each step grows with the step number, so the total input of a run grows roughly with the square of the step count.


The chart models one agent run with a 3,000-token fixed prefix (system prompt plus tool definitions) and 1,500 new tokens of history per step. One line resends the full history. The other caps the history at the last three steps and summarizes the rest.


At 5 steps the two lines are close. At 20 steps the uncapped run sends 345,000 input tokens, about 2.4 times the capped run. Agents that run for dozens of steps are where most surprise bills come from, which matches Anthropic's finding that agents use about 4 times the tokens of chat. Prompt caching softens the curve, because the fixed prefix and the older history are a stable prefix. It does not remove it, because the newest steps are always fresh input.


Part of the agent prompt Sent on Main lever


System prompt Every step Cache it and keep it byte-stable


Tool definitions Every step Attach only the tools this step can use, in a fixed order


Conversation and tool history Every step, and it grows[Context compaction](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai-agents/context-compaction) , drop raw tool results


Retrieved documents Steps that retrieve Top passages only, not whole files


Reasoning tokens Every step, billed as output Lower[reasoning effort](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/reasoning-effort) on easy steps


### Tool calls multiply the bill


**Each tool call costs a full model step: the model writes the call as output, your code runs the tool, and the result returns as input on the next step.** Ten tool calls mean at least ten more model calls, and each one resends the history. Four habits keep tool-heavy agents cheap:


1. **Return compact tool results.** Send the fields the model needs, not raw HTML or a full JSON dump. A 6,000-token web page cut to a 400-token summary saves that difference on every later step.
2. **Batch independent calls.** When the API supports parallel[function calling](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/function-calling) , let the model request several lookups in one step instead of one step per lookup.
3. **Keep tool schemas short.** Every tool definition rides along on every call. A tool description of three sentences works as well as a page of text for most tools.
4. **Stop the loop on purpose.** Give the agent a step limit and a token budget per run, and a clear "done" condition. The[agent loop](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai-agents/agent-loop) entry covers how loops end, and[agent memory](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai-agents/agent-memory) covers what to keep between runs instead of in the prompt.


Multi-agent designs multiply all of this. Anthropic measured multi-agent systems at about 15 times the tokens of chat, so use several agents only when the task really splits into parallel parts.[Multi-agent systems](https://www.taskade.com/blog/multi-agent-systems) and[what AI agents are](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-are-ai-agents) cover when the extra agents earn their cost.

## A Worked Example: Cutting a $1,800 Monthly Bill to $231


**Here is how the levers combine on one realistic workload: a support assistant that answers 100,000 requests per month.** Each request carries a 4,000-token stable prefix (system prompt plus reference documents), a 500-token variable question, and a 300-token answer. The example uses illustrative rates of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with Anthropic-style cache rates (0.1x read, 1.25x write).


**Baseline.** Input is 100,000 × 4,500 = 450 million tokens × $3 = $1,350. Output is 100,000 × 300 = 30 million tokens × $15 = $450. Total: **$1,800 per month** .


**Step 1: prompt caching.** The 4,000-token prefix is 400 million tokens per month. Assume steady traffic keeps the cache warm, so 99 percent of prefix tokens are cache reads and 1 percent are cache writes.


- Cache reads: 396 million × $0.30 = $118.80
- Cache writes: 4 million × $3.75 = $15.00
- Variable question: 50 million × $3 = $150.00
- Output: $450.00 (unchanged)
- Total: **$733.80** , a 59 percent cut


**Step 2: model routing.** Send 70 percent of requests to a model whose rates are one fifth of the main model's, and keep 30 percent on the main model. The routed share costs 0.7 × $733.80 ÷ 5 = $102.73. The main share costs 0.3 × $733.80 = $220.14. Total: **$322.87** , an 82 percent cut.


**Step 3: output length control.** After routing, the output part of the bill is $450 × (0.3 + 0.7 ÷ 5) = $198. Clear length instructions bring the average answer from 300 to 200 tokens, which removes a third of that: $66. Total: **$256.87** , an 86 percent cut.


**Step 4: batch the nightly work.** Suppose 20 percent of requests are nightly summaries that nobody reads until morning. Moving that slice to a batch API saves 0.2 × $256.87 × 0.5 = $25.69. Total: **$231.18** , an 87 percent cut.


Step Arithmetic Monthly cost Cut vs baseline


Baseline $1,350 input + $450 output $1,800.00 0 percent


+ Prompt caching $118.80 + $15.00 + $150.00 + $450.00 $733.80 59 percent


+ Route 70 percent to a 5x cheaper model $102.73 + $220.14 $322.87 82 percent


+ Cut answers from 300 to 200 tokens $322.87 − $66.00 $256.87 86 percent


+ Batch 20 percent of requests $256.87 − $25.69 $231.18 87 percent


Three lessons come out of the arithmetic. First, caching does the heavy lifting on input-heavy workloads, because the prefix is 89 percent of all input tokens here. Second, after caching, output becomes the largest line on the bill (it is $450 of the $733.80), which is why output control matters more than most guides admit. Third, the later steps save fewer dollars because they act on a smaller bill. Structured outputs would remove any retries on top of this; we left retries out of the baseline to keep the math clean. If 5 percent of calls had retried before, strict schemas would remove almost all of that extra 5 percent.


Your own figures will differ, but the shape holds: **cache first, route second, then cap output, trim, batch, and constrain.** To turn this into a per-task view, divide each line by 100,000: the baseline costs 1.8 cents per answered request, and the final setup costs about 0.23 cents. That per-task number is the one to track week to week, as[what one AI task really costs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-cost-per-task) explains.

A prompt that is too long is the single most common root cause on this list. Most teams find a stale example block, an unused tool, or a full document where three passages would do. The[context window](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/context-window) and[context rot](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/context-rot) entries explain why a shorter prompt is often more accurate too.

## When Cost Techniques Do Not Help


**Cost techniques fail when the saving is smaller than the engineering time, or when the workload has nothing the technique can act on.** Five cases come up often:


- **Very low volume.** If the whole bill is a few hundred dollars a month, a week of router work costs more than a year of savings. Pick the cheapest model that passes your eval and stop there.
- **No repeated prefix.** Prompt caching does nothing for one-off prompts that share no opening text.
- **Only the frontier model passes.** If a smaller model fails your eval on most tasks, a cascade pays twice on most tasks. Spend the effort on output length and context instead.
- **Every answer is interactive.** Batch APIs and off-peak schedules need work that can wait. A live chat cannot.
- **Answers must be exact and current.** Semantic caching risks a stale or wrong answer in domains such as prices, policies, and medical or legal facts.

## Frequently Asked Questions


How do you reduce LLM API costs?


Start with prompt caching, because most production prompts repeat a long fixed prefix. Anthropic bills cache reads at 0.1x the base input price, and OpenAI discounts cached input by up to 95 percent. Then route easy tasks to a cheaper model, cap output length, trim the context, and move non-urgent work to a batch API at 50 percent off. Measure cost per completed task before and after each change. Combined, these levers often cut a typical bill by 80 percent or more.


How much can prompt caching save?


Prompt caching can remove up to 90 to 95 percent of the cost of the cached part of a prompt. Anthropic charges cache reads at 0.1x base input, with a write premium of 1.25x for the 5-minute cache and 2x for the 1-hour cache. OpenAI caches automatically and discounts cached input by up to 95 percent, and on GPT-5.6 and later, reads cost 0.1x on most models with a 1.25x write. A 4,000-token stable prefix with a 500-token question cuts input cost by roughly 80 percent.


How do OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google prompt caching differ?


All three match on the prompt prefix, but they turn on differently. OpenAI caching is on by default for prompts of 1,024 tokens or more. Anthropic caching uses cache breakpoints, up to four per request, or automatic caching, with a 5-minute default lifetime that refreshes on every read. Google Gemini turns on implicit caching by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer models and passes the saving through automatically. In every case, a change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it.


When should I use a batch API instead of real-time calls?


Use a batch API for any work that does not need an answer within seconds: nightly reports, bulk classification, data enrichment, document tagging, and evaluation runs. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google batch APIs charge 50 percent of the standard price for input and output. OpenAI batches complete within 24 hours and take up to 50,000 requests. Anthropic says most batches finish in under 1 hour and accepts up to 100,000 requests. Keep interactive, user-facing calls on the standard endpoint.


What is model routing and how much does it save?


Model routing sends each task to the cheapest model that meets the quality bar, and escalates only hard tasks to a frontier model. The RouteLLM research reported cost cuts of more than 2x in some cases without lower answer quality, and FrugalGPT reported up to 98 percent lower cost while it matched the best single model. Your saving depends on your task mix. Routing 70 percent of traffic to a model five times cheaper cuts that bill by 56 percent.


Why do output tokens cost more than input tokens?


Output tokens cost more because the model writes them one at a time during the decode phase, while it reads all input tokens in parallel during prefill. Decode keeps the GPU busy longer for each token. On the DeepSeek API, output costs 3x the cache-miss input rate, and many frontier models charge 4x to 5x. Reasoning tokens are usually billed as output too, so capping output length and reasoning effort is a direct cost lever.[Inference-as-a-Service](https://www.taskade.com/blog/inference-as-a-service) explains the serving stack behind these prices.


What is the difference between prompt caching and semantic caching?


Prompt caching happens at the provider. The model still runs, but the provider bills the repeated prompt prefix at a lower rate. Semantic caching happens in your application. You store past answers with an embedding of the question, and when a new question is close enough in meaning, you return the stored answer and make no model call at all. Prompt caching suits long shared instructions. Semantic caching suits repeated questions, such as support FAQs.


Does DeepSeek charge less at off-peak hours?


Yes. Since 2026-08-16, the DeepSeek API bills at a peak rate from 01:00 to 04:00 and 06:00 to 10:00 UTC on weekdays, and at half that rate at all other times, including weekends and Chinese public holidays. For deepseek-v4-pro, peak rates are $1.32 input and $3.96 output per million tokens, and off-peak rates are $0.66 and $1.98. Cache hits cost $0.044 at peak and $0.022 off-peak. About 79 percent of the hours in a week are off-peak.


How do I measure whether a cost optimization worked?


Track cost per completed task, not cost per token. Per-token prices keep falling, but calls per task keep climbing, so a per-token view can look flat while your bill rises. Log the input, cached, output, and retry token counts that each provider returns, group them by task type, and compare a week before and a week after each change. Also measure task success rate. For a 20-task measurement protocol, see[what one AI task really costs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-cost-per-task) .


Can I combine prompt caching and batching?


Yes. Caching lowers the price of repeated input tokens, and batching applies a flat 50 percent discount for delayed delivery, so the two stack. Anthropic states that cache multipliers stack with the Batch API discount, and it recommends the 1-hour cache for batches with shared context, because a batch can take longer than 5 minutes. OpenAI flex processing bills at Batch API rates, and prompt caching discounts apply on top.


Does a bigger context window make my LLM app more expensive?


A bigger context window does not raise the price per token, but filling it does. You pay for every input token on every call, so a long chat history or a full document set multiplies input cost. Long context can also lower answer quality, an effect called context rot. Send only what the task needs: retrieve the top passages, summarize old turns, and drop stale tool results. Shorter context is cheaper and often more accurate.

How do I calculate the cost of an LLM API request?


Multiply each token type by its own rate and add the results: uncached input tokens times the input rate, cached input tokens times the cache read rate, cache write tokens times the write rate, and output tokens times the output rate, all divided by one million. Multiply by requests per month for the bill, and by one plus your retry rate. A 6,000-token prompt with a 5,000-token cached prefix and a 400-token answer, at $2 input, $0.10 cached input, and $10 output per million tokens, costs about 0.65 cents per call, against 1.6 cents with no caching.


How do I reduce LLM API costs for AI agents?


An agent resends its growing history on every step, so cap the number of steps and the tokens per run, compact old turns into a summary, drop raw tool results once they are used, and attach only the tools the current step needs, because every tool definition is sent on every call. Keep the system prompt and tool list stable so that they cache, route easy steps to a smaller model, and move deterministic work such as validation and formatting into code.[AI agent cost optimization](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization) goes deeper.


Is self-hosting an open-weight model cheaper than using an API?


Only at high and steady volume. A hosted API bills per token, so idle time costs nothing. A self-hosted model bills per GPU hour whether the GPUs are busy or not, and a large open-weight model needs a full multi-GPU node. The Kimi K3 checkpoint, for example, is about 1.56 TB, which fits one 8-GPU B300 node but not an 8-GPU B200 node. Divide your GPU cost per hour by the tokens you actually serve per hour, add staff time, and compare that to the API price.


Does the same open-weight model cost the same on every host?


No. Each host that serves the same open weights sets its own prices, cache support, and speed. On Artificial Analysis on 2026-10-20, Kimi K3 hosts ranged from about 42 to about 422 output tokens per second, roughly a 10x spread, and the listed blended prices ranged from about $1.72 to about $4.62 per million tokens. Compare the cached-input price, rate limits, speed, and data terms before you pick a host.[No-code builders that run open-weight models](https://www.taskade.com/blog/open-model-builders) shows which tools let you choose.


Why is my LLM API bill higher than expected?


The usual causes are a broken prompt cache, an agent history that grows and is resent on every call, retries after malformed or cut-off answers, hidden reasoning tokens billed as output, long-context price tiers, and a tokenizer that counts more tokens for the same text. Anthropic, for example, says its newer tokenizer produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text. Log input, cached, output, and reasoning tokens for each call, group them by feature, and look for the line that grew.


How does prompt caching work on hybrid models like Kimi K3?


Kimi K3 mixes 69 linear-attention (KDA) layers with 24 Gated MLA layers. The MLA layers keep a per-token cache that can resume at the exact token, but the KDA layers keep one fixed-size state per sequence, so the server resumes from the nearest saved state checkpoint and prefills the rest again. Prefix caching on hybrid models is therefore coarser. Keep the shared prefix long and identical so that the saved checkpoints cover most of it.
